figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of producing a quantized representation x̂ of an EEG signal x using 𝑀 = 4 codebook levels. The length 𝑘 of the signals is 100 (equaling to 200 ms at our 500 Hz sampling rate), i.e. the same we use for the prediction horizon. The original and residual signals (in yellow) are mapped to the closest codebook elements (green signals) at the respective codebook levels. First, we find the closest match (highlighted with red) for x from the first codebook (𝐶𝐵1). Then, we calculate the difference between the closest match x̂1 and x to form the first residual signal x2 that is then correspondingly mapped to the closest item in 𝐶𝐵2. This process is repeated until we have selected one codebook item from all four codebooks. The final quantized signal x̂ is then formed as the sum of the selected items. The rightmost column shows x̂ (at the bottom) as well as the intermediate sums.

Figure 2: REVBRAIN is composed of an encoder and 𝑀 prediction heads. The encoder turns the input into a latent representation z that the heads use to produce the probability distributions over the codebook indices {𝑖1, . . . , 𝑖𝑀}. The first head produces the first index 𝑖1 using only z. The following heads then get as inputs both z and all previously predicted indices (indicated with gray arrows). After all the indices are generated, they are used to retrieve the corresponding waveforms {x̂1, . . . , x̂𝑀} from the codebooks, and the final prediction is defined as their sum x = ∑𝑀 𝑚=1 x̂𝑚.

Figure 3: REVBRAIN (a) achieved a notable speed-up over WaveNet in inference latency while (b) also reducing the prediction error. (a) The figure shows median latencies over 100 iterations for generating 1, 10, and 100 samples per input. The speed-up was the greatest when generating 100 samples (3170×) and the smallest when generating just 1 sample (52×). (b) The figure shows the mean absolute errors (MAE) on the test data as functions of time. The predictions for both models were formed as the mean of 10 predicted samples. Due to the delay caused by the bandpass filter, the prediction starts 128 ms in the “past” and the true prediction begins at 𝑇𝑖𝑚𝑒 = 0 (grey vertical line). The mean absolute errors of the true predictions were 2.4 ± 2.4 µV (REVBRAIN) and 2.6 ± 2.7 µV (WaveNet).

Figure 4: Figure (a) depicts the phase bins used for the phase detection: [315°, 45°), [45°, 135°), [135°, 225°), [225°, 315°), roughly corresponding to a peak, falling flank, trough, and rising flank. Figure (b) shows the results of the probabilistic phase detection. The precision rises and recall falls as the threshold is increased—with thresholds of over 90 % prediction was almost never done, but the few that were received close to perfect precision.

Figure 5: The median latencies over 100 iterations for each step in the real-time usage pipeline (top row) and for the whole pipeline (bottom row). The measured signal is first band-pass filtered on the CPU, and the filtered signal is moved to the GPU. Then, the model inference and decision making steps are performed on the GPU. Finally, the binary decision flag is moved back to the CPU to communicate to the system whether to take action or not. Most of the time was consumed by the inference and decision making steps, while the other steps (band-pass filtering and moving to and from GPU) were extremely fast.

Figure 6: (a) The Transformer head (TF-REVBRAIN) increased the inference latencies compared to the MLP-based heads (REVBRAIN), though also this version of the model achieved real-time inference with the smaller sample sizes. (b) The Transformer head resulted in a marginal improvement of 0.01 µV in mean absolute error (MAE) on the test set compared to REVBRAIN.

Table 1: Layers and layer dimensions of each prediction head of REVBRAIN. The number after an embedding layer signals the embedding dimension. The values for the fully connected (FC) layers correspond to input and output features, respectively. The number of input features for the first FC layer of each head is composed of the dimension of z plus the embedding dimensions of the current and previous levels.

Table 2: Training hyperparameters of REVBRAIN, TF-REVBRAIN, and WaveNet, and the model dimensions of the encoder, WaveNet, and the Transformer-based prediction head (TF head). As shown, the encoder and WaveNet share the same parameters. Note that we use a single Transformer as the prediction head in TFREVBRAIN, and the row “Heads” refers to the number of heads in a single Transformer layer. Final FCs (𝑀 = 5) are the linear layers after the Transformer.

Table 4: RVQ model performance with varying codebook sizes (𝑁) and numbers of codebook levels (𝑀). The reported values are mean absolute quantization errors (µV) over the whole 200 ms window on the train and validation subjects. Bolded values correspond to the errors of our chosen codebook size (𝑁 = 512) and number of codebook levels (𝑀 = 5).

Figure 8: Examples of 10 predicted samples with (a) and without (b) the inputrelative encoding of the outputs. The generated samples without the centering step tend to have small offsets relative to the input in the beginning of the prediction, whereas applying the centering ensures that the start of the forecast is aligned with the input time series.
